You talk about the unreal past at B2 level: the conditional perfect (habría hecho), “si + pluperfect subjunctive” (si me hubiera quedado), mixed conditionals (si no me hubiera ido, hoy no estaría aquí), “de + perfect infinitive” (de haberlo sabido) and “ojalá + hubiera”.
If I had stayed, I would be a different person today.
Had I known, I would have opened the café under another name.
If only I had brought my camera.
If I were braver, I would have stayed.
To form the conditional perfect (habría hecho, habrías dicho) and the pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera hecho, hubiese dicho).
To build hypotheses about the past: si + hubiera + participle → habría + participle.
To use mixed conditionals: a past cause with a present effect (si no me hubiera ido, hoy no estaría aquí) and the reverse (si fuera más valiente, me habría quedado).
To use “de + perfect infinitive” (de haberlo sabido) and “ojalá + hubiera” for regrets.
To recognise “hubiera” used instead of “habría” in the main clause in everyday speech.

6 October, evening, El Mostrador café. Tomorrow the plaque will be unveiled. Ecaterina sees Faustino, the bookseller from the Cuesta de Moyano, for the first time in almost forty years. Lola brings them coffee.
If someone had told me forty years ago that I’d see you again, I wouldn’t have believed it.
Nor would I, Faustino. Here: I owed you for a Neruda book. With interest.
Five hundred pesetas? If you had paid me in 1985, we wouldn’t have this excuse to see each other now.
Ecaterina, would you have stayed in Madrid if your mother hadn’t fallen ill?
Possibly. And if I had stayed, I’d be a different person today. Perhaps happier. Perhaps not.
If you had stayed, Gil would have stolen even more of my customers. He was unbearably happy.
Had I known, I’d have opened the café under another name: La Lámpara.
No, Lola. If it were called La Lámpara, it would be a museum. This way it’s a café where people read. He would have liked that better.
If only I’d brought my camera. I would have taken this photo too.
Don’t worry: Andrei is at the door. He’s already taken it.

The “h” is silent: [u-BIE-ra], [u-BIE-se]. The diphthong “ie” is a single stressed syllable.
The stress falls on the “í”, which forms a separate syllable: a-BRÍ-a (three syllables, not two). Likewise: sería, tendría, haría.
It is linked into a single group, without the “h”: [dea-BER-lo-sa-BI-do]. “de” and “ha-” merge.
1. The forms: habría hecho and hubiera hecho
The “-ra” forms (hubiera) and the “-se” forms (hubiese) are equivalent. “Hubiera” is more common in speech.
Something that did NOT happen in the past, and its consequence, also in the past:
If you had called me, I would have waited for you.
If she had said goodbye in 1987, everything would have been different.
In speech you often hear «Si lo hubiera sabido, lo hubiera dicho» (hubiera in both halves). It’s correct and very common. But NEVER «Si lo habría sabido…» ✗: the conditional never follows “si”.
Si no me hubiera ido, hoy no estaría aquí.
Si fuera más valiente, me habría quedado.
Ask yourself: WHEN is the condition and WHEN is the result? Each half keeps its own tense. “Si no hubiera llovido ayer” (past) + “hoy el campo estaría seco” (present).
4. De + perfect infinitive and ojalá + hubiera
Had you arrived earlier, you would have met him.
If only I had told him in time.
“De + haber + participle” is a short, elegant alternative to “si + hubiera”. “Ojalá + hubiera” expresses a regret: something that can no longer be changed.
“If I had known, I would have come.”
Si lo habría sabido, hubiera venido.
“If I hadn’t left, I wouldn’t be here today.”
Si no me fuera, hoy no habría estado aquí.
Si no me habría ido, hoy no estaría aquí.

On Sunday 5 October, the supplement hit the kiosks with the photo of the lamp across a full page. Underneath, in small print, Begoña had written a two-line caption: “Calle de las Huertas, two in the morning. A bookshop that no longer exists still has its light on.” Lola opened El Mostrador at eight, as on every Sunday. By ten there was a queue in the street. By eleven she had run out of milk. At twelve she called Marta, on the verge of a nervous breakdown.

Marta and Andrei arrived within ten minutes. Marta started washing cups and Andrei, who had never served a coffee in his life, ended up behind the bar. The customers recognised him from the photo on the supplement’s flap and asked him to sign their newspapers. Andrei went so red that Lola had to send him to the back room for more glasses. From there, through the half-open door, he watched people photographing the lamp with their phones, in silence, as if in a church.

At midday Faustino arrived, with the supplement under his arm and his Sunday beret. He sat at the table at the back, ordered a black coffee and spent a long time watching the people coming and going. When Lola brought him his coffee, he said: “If Gil saw this, he’d pull down the shutters so as not to have to serve so many people. He was a very good bookseller, but a very bad shopkeeper.” Then he paid, left an enormous tip and said he would be back the next day, because he had an appointment with an old debt.

That evening, the series was the most-read item on the newspaper’s website. The agency’s inbox received more than three hundred emails: people who remembered La Lámpara, people who had bought their first book there, people who just wanted to say thank you. At eleven, Begoña sent Andrei a one-word message: “Good.” When Lucas saw it, he explained very seriously that this was even rarer than “not bad”, and that in five years he had never seen her write it to anyone.

On Monday the 6th, the club landed at Barajas: Ecaterina, Ana, Mihai, Rosa Elena, Costel and Mrs Florica, who was getting on a plane for the first time at seventy-two. She had spent the take-off gripping Costel’s hand so hard she left marks. But on landing she declared that, had she known flying was so calm, she would have travelled forty years ago. Costel, rubbing his hand, replied that, had he known she squeezed so hard, he would have sat in another row.

At the arrivals gate, Andrei was waiting for them with Marta. He hugged them all, one by one. And then he saw, behind Costel, a tall man with glasses and a small suitcase trying unsuccessfully to hide. It was his father. Señor Dan had bought the ticket without telling anyone except Ana, who had kept the secret for three weeks. Andrei froze. His father shrugged and said: “If I hadn’t come, your mother wouldn’t have let me back into the house.”

In the kitchen on the calle del Prado, Mrs Florica opened her suitcase like someone opening a treasure chest: six jars of zacuscă, two kilos of frozen sarmale, a cozonac wrapped in a tea towel and a jar of gherkins. Marta didn’t know where to put it all. An hour later Carmen arrived with a tortilla the size of a car wheel. The two cooks looked at each other, examined each other’s dishes with professional suspicion and, after tasting, shook hands. From that moment on they understood each other perfectly, although they didn’t speak the same language.

Meanwhile, Juan confessed in front of everyone a secret his family had known for forty years: he had never been able to flip a tortilla without breaking it. Rosa Elena offered to try. Carmen put a small tortilla in the pan, held the little girl’s hands in hers and they counted to three together. The tortilla flew, spun in the air and landed whole, perfect, on the plate. Juan gave her a standing ovation and declared Rosa Elena an honorary Spaniard. She replied that she already was, because her grandmother was from Madrid.

That evening, at El Mostrador, Ecaterina saw Faustino again for the first time since 1987. They recognised each other at once, although both had changed a great deal. Ecaterina took an old envelope out of her bag. Inside was a five-hundred-peseta note she had kept for forty years in the same drawer as the letter. It was the price of the Neruda book she had never paid him for. Faustino looked at it, laughed until tears came to his eyes and said he had no intention of spending it: he was going to frame it and hang it in his stall.

Ecaterina had also brought him a copy of the Romanian edition of the novel, with a dedication written the night before at the hotel: “For Faustino, the best competitor Andrés ever had, who took the most beautiful photo of my life without my knowing.” Faustino read it twice, his glasses on the tip of his nose, and said he didn’t understand a word of Romanian, but he would never sell that book, not even if he were offered a million pesetas.

They talked until late. Lola asked Ecaterina whether she would have stayed in Madrid if her mother hadn’t fallen ill. Ecaterina took a while to answer. She said it was possible, and that if she had stayed, she would be a different person today, perhaps happier, perhaps not. Faustino said that, in any case, if she had stayed, Gil would have stolen even more of his customers, because when he was in love he sold twice as much. Everyone laughed, and for a moment the lamp at the back seemed to shine a little brighter.

Ecaterina woke at five in the morning. She had written the speech in Bucharest, a whole page, and on the plane she had cut it down to half. That dawn, sitting on the hotel bed, she rewrote it four times, shorter each time, until only four sentences were left. She remembered Andrés saying that good speeches should fit on a bookmark. She copied the four sentences onto the back of the La Lámpara bookmark Lola had given her in May, and they just fitted.

Tuesday 7 October dawned cool and clear. At eleven, the local police closed calle de las Huertas to traffic. On the façade of El Mostrador, at eye level, a blue cloth covered the plaque, with a golden cord hanging down to the ground. Lola had brought all the café’s chairs out onto the pavement, although they weren’t much use: by a quarter to twelve there were more than two hundred people in the street, and almost all of them were standing.

Everyone was there. Pilar had arrived from Seville that very morning. Carmen and Juan, in their Sunday best. Faustino, in his best beret, which turned out to be red. The twins from Lavapiés, arguing about whether the plaque was crooked. Begoña and Lucas, cameras round their necks. The director of the fair, several retired booksellers, neighbours, customers and dozens of strangers who had seen the photo in the supplement. And in the front row, the club from Bucharest, with Rosa Elena sitting on Mihai’s shoulders so she could see.

While they were waiting, Rosa Elena went up to Begoña, who had the biggest camera in the whole street, and showed her her own. She asked if she wanted to see her photos. Begoña, who almost never smiled, crouched down and went through the photos on the little screen one by one, very seriously, as she did with Andrei’s: the covered plaque, Faustino’s red beret, the councillor’s shoes, a pigeon. When she had finished, she gave the camera back and said: “Not bad.” Lucas, who had heard, covered his face with his hands.

The councillor for culture spoke first, in the language Ecaterina loved most: “Following the approval of the application submitted by the interested parties, and once the corresponding formalities have been concluded, we proceed to the unveiling of the commemorative plaque.” Ecaterina smiled at hearing so many nouns together. Beside her, Costel whispered, very proudly, that he had understood everything, word for word. Ana whispered back that in that case he had as good as passed the November exam.

Then Marta spoke, very briefly. She said that if her grandfather had known so many people were going to come, he would have put on the linen jacket Pilar bought him for the fair, and would probably have tried to sell each of them a book. Pilar said just one sentence, looking at Ecaterina: “If my father saw you now, he’d say you’ve finally come back for your book and for your light.” Ecaterina had to take off her glasses for a moment.

Then it was her turn. She took out a folded piece of paper, unfolded it carefully and read, slowly, in her usual firm voice, a four-sentence speech. She spoke of what would have happened if she had stayed, if she had said goodbye, if she had posted the letter. She said that if she had stayed, perhaps she would have been happy, but then she wouldn’t be there with all of them, and that plaque wouldn’t exist. And she finished by saying she had no regrets, because both lives, the one she had and the one she didn’t, had the same light.

Then she took the hand of Rosa Elena, who had climbed down from her father’s shoulders, and together they pulled the golden cord. The blue cloth fell slowly. Underneath appeared a simple bronze plaque, with large letters: “Here stood the La Lámpara bookshop. Its bookseller, Andrés Gil, left the light on.” For a few seconds nobody moved. Then Faustino took off his red beret, and everyone else, without any signal, began to clap.

Costel was crying, as was to be expected. Mrs Florica crossed herself three times. Juan, who never said anything, said “olé” under his breath. Señor Dan, for once, was taking photos with his phone, while his son, two metres away, took them with a real camera. Rosa Elena took out hers, photographed the plaque and then asked, very seriously, why the letters on plaques were always so serious. Nobody knew what to answer.

Lola had a surprise ready. When the applause died down, she went into the café and switched on a second lamp, a small one with a green shade, which she had hung in the window overnight, just below the plaque. She explained that the one inside could only be seen if you came up to the glass, and that she wanted the light, from that day on, to be visible from the street too, from far away, from any corner. She promised to leave it on every night for as long as she had the café.

Pilar came over to Ecaterina while people queued to photograph the plaque. She reminded her of the invitation to Seville and suggested a date: April, when the book came out, to launch it in a small bookshop in the Triana district that her father had known as a young man. Ecaterina asked whether she was saying it out of politeness. Pilar replied that if it were out of politeness, she would have said it by email. She was saying it in person because, had he been able to, her father would have been in the front row at that launch.

They had lunch at Carmen and Juan’s in Lavapiés. On the table there was tortilla, sarmale, zacuscă, cozonac and jamón, and nobody dared say which they liked best. Begoña, sitting next to Costel, talked to him for half an hour about photography and wars, and Costel answered without a single mistake. At the end, she told him he would pass the exam without any trouble. Costel promised that, if he passed, he would invite everyone to Madrid again. Mihai raised his glass and proposed a toast: “To the lights that someone leaves on.”

Over dessert, Señor Dan asked to speak, something he had never done. He announced, blushing, that he too had registered for the DELE B2 exam in November, and that he hadn’t told anyone in case he failed. Costel, who had taken B1 with him, jumped up from his chair. He told him that if he had said so earlier, they would have studied together all summer, and that now they would have to make up for lost time. They agreed to study together on Thursdays, in the lorry’s cab, which according to Costel was the best office in Romania.

In the afternoon, Andrei took his father to the Toledo bridge. Señor Dan spent half an hour examining the arches, touching the stone and pacing out distances. Then he leaned on the railing, looked at the river and said that if he had known Madrid was so beautiful, he would have come much earlier. He told Andrei that his mother had bought five copies of the supplement, framed the photo of the lamp and hung it in the living room, right above the television, so that nobody could avoid seeing it.

Before leaving, Begoña took Andrei aside, by the door. She told him the internship ended in February, and that after that the agency would need someone. She promised nothing. She only said that if he hadn’t brought her that photo, she wouldn’t be telling him this, and that if he kept looking at the city the way he had that month, they would talk in February. Andrei didn’t know what to say. His father, who had heard everything from the stairs, did: he slapped him on the back and told him, in Romanian, to buy himself a coat, because it was cold in Madrid in winter too.

That night, very late, Ecaterina asked Ana to go with her one last time to calle de las Huertas. The street was empty. The plaque shone under the green light of the lamp in the window, and at the back of the café the other one could be seen, the one that was always there. Ecaterina read the plaque once more, quietly, word by word. Then she said: “If I had stayed, I would have had one life. I left and had another. I don’t know which would have been better. I only know that both have brought me here.”

She touched the plaque with her fingertips, as she had touched the green sign on the night of the funeral. Then she turned to leave. But after a few steps she stopped, turned round again and stood for a moment looking at the light, face on, unhurried. Ana understood what she was doing and said nothing. In 1987, Ecaterina had left that street without looking back. This time she left slowly, watching the lamp until she turned the corner. Like someone who, at last, says goodbye properly.
